analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits and requires the wealthiest workers to pay payroll taxes on earnings above $400,000.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 202 House Democrats, never received a committee vote or a floor vote in either chamber before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would boost every Social Security check, use a cost-of-living index that tracks what retirees actually buy, raise minimum benefits above poverty for long-career low earners, add caregiver credits, repeal the 5-month disability waiting period, and repeal rules that cut benefits for certain state and local government retirees. To pay for it, workers earning above $400,000 and their employers would pay Social Security taxes on those higher earnings, a group currently exempt above a much lower wage cap.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security beneficiaries: current retirees and disability recipients get a higher formula benefit and a faster cost-of-living adjustment; long-career low earners get a minimum benefit tied to the poverty line; caregivers get work credits; disabled applicants get benefits immediately instead of waiting five months; state and local government retirees no longer lose benefits under the two offset rules; adult children in college under 26 and children raised by grandparents get access.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security retirees, disabled workers, caregivers

how_it_helps.text: Increases the first benefit formula tier from 90 to 93 percent of average earnings, an across-the-board increase for 2022 through 2026 [S3].

Switches the annual cost-of-living adjustment to the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers (CPI-E), which reflects retirees' spending, and directs the Bureau of Labor Statistics to publish it monthly [S3].
Sets a new minimum benefit scaled to years of work, reaching 125 percent of the federal poverty guideline for workers with 30 or more years of coverage [S3].
Raises the income thresholds at which Social Security benefits become taxable and cuts the top inclusion rate, reducing income tax on many beneficiaries [S3].
Improves survivor benefits for widows and widowers in two-earner households and adds benefits that grow for beneficiaries 15 or more years past initial eligibility [S3].
Grants up to 60 months of deemed wages for uncompensated caregiving of young children or chronically dependent relatives [S3].

Eliminates the five-month waiting period for disability benefits and replaces the cliff-edge earnings cutoff with a $1-for-$2 benefit reduction so disabled beneficiaries keep more when they work [S3].

Repeals the Government Pension Offset and Windfall Elimination Provision, which reduce or eliminate earned Social Security benefits for roughly three million retired public employees (number per widely reported CRS/AARP analyses of WEP/GOP populations; the repeal itself is in the bill text) [S3].

Adds work credits for uncompensated caregiving of young children or chronically dependent relatives, and extends child benefits to post-secondary students under 26 and to children living with grandparents or other relatives [S3].
Bars SSA field, hearing, and rural office closures and requires mailed annual account statements unless the recipient opts out [S3].

analysis.who_pays: High earners above $400,000 and their employers: the bill removes the current taxable-earnings cap for wages above $400,000, applies the 12.4 percent payroll tax to that income, and counts earnings above $400,000 in the benefit formula at a low 1 percent marginal rate. The added revenue goes to the newly consolidated Social Security Trust Fund, which combines the existing Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability funds.

drawbacks.text: The tax increase is regressive in form: payroll taxes hit earners at every wage, so raising the payroll tax on workers between the current cap and $400,000 costs them more, even though their benefits rise little because only 1 percent of excess earnings counts toward benefits [S3].
The bill does not say how the increase is financed or scored: no CRS or CBO estimate is cited, and opponents could argue revenue is insufficient to make benefits permanent.

Strongest good-faith objection: benefit increases are stacked across many provisions (formula bump, CPI-E, minimum benefit, 15-year bump, caregiver credits), making the package expensive to score and, by critic accounts, insufficient to extend trust fund solvency to 2100.

Repealing the Government Pension Offset and Windfall Elimination Provision costs the trust fund money and was widely opposed by unions and public-employee groups as a costly giveaway; Congress later instead enacted a scaled-back WEP fix in the Social Security Fairness Act of 2025.
The bill mandates mailed statements and bars SSA office closures without a stated funding mechanism for SSA administrative costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit increases are real and broad, and the tax change falls entirely above the $400,000 line, so the trade is largely between high earners and beneficiaries. But the package stacks many benefit expansions and applies a strict payroll-tax increase to earners just above the cap while giving them only a 1 percent benefit return, which critics view as a large and slow-growing tax on high earners. Whether the combined revenue truly extends solvency long-term depends on projections not provided in the bill text.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced October 26, 2021 and referred to three committees; the House Ways and Means Social Security Subcommittee and Health Subcommittee took no recorded action, and no committee vote, floor vote, or Senate companion action occurred before the 117th Congress ended January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Introduced by Representative John B. Larson (D-CT) on October 26, 2021 with 202 Democratic cosponsors, including House Ways and Means Chair Richard Neal and Majority Whip James Clyburn [S3, S4].

Referred to House Ways and Means, Education and Labor, and Energy and Commerce; Ways and Means then referred it to its Social Security Subcommittee and Energy and Commerce to its Health Subcommittee [S1, S5].
No further action was recorded: no hearings, markups, committee or floor votes, or Senate companion in the 117th Congress [S5].
The bill died at adjournment on January 3, 2023; an identically named successor bill was introduced in the 118th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners above the $400,000 payroll tax line and their employers keep the current tax exemption on earnings above the existing cap. Social Security beneficiaries receive none of the proposed benefit increases or offset repeals.

for.name: Rep. John B. Larson (D-CT)
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Social Security Subcommittee Chair
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and built the Democratic cosponsor bloc

for.name: Rep. Richard Neal (D-MA)
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor; as Ways and Means chair held jurisdiction over the bill but did not schedule a markup

sides.party_line_note: All 202 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsors and no recorded opposition because the bill never reached a vote.

industries.note: Would pay the 12.4 percent Social Security payroll tax on earnings above $400,000, ending the current exemption above the lower cap. This group would bear the entire revenue cost of the expanded benefits.

industries.industry: U.S. Social Security Administration (field offices, rural contact stations)
industries.note: Bars SSA field, hearing, and rural office closures and requires mailed account statements, locking in physical SSA service infrastructure and administrative spending.

industries.industry: State and local government pension systems
industries.note: Repeal of the Government Pension Offset and Windfall Elimination Provision would remove offsets these systems rely on and would raise federal outlays for retired public employees.
